metaDescription: Spoken English answers for QA Automation interviews. Short sentences, as I would say them.

nav.commandHint: Type a page or a question.

title: Interview Q&A
intro: These are answers I can say out loud. Short sentences. Simple words. I keep real tool names: fixtures, storageState, 401. This is not the same English as the CV page.

items.a: I am a Senior General QA Engineer. I have more than five years in testing. First I was a manual QA. Then I moved to automation. My main tools are TypeScript, Playwright, Postman, SQL and Jenkins. I test UI and API. I also build test frameworks and run tests in CI. I have FinTech experience. I worked on a B2B payment platform in Access and Identity.
I am in Ukraine. Dnipro. I work remote. I can relocate.

items.q: Why do you want a new job?
items.a: I want a challenging product. I want more impact on automation and QA processes.

items.q: Why did you leave your last job?
items.a: I left because I was mobilized. Now I am available.
I started IT at university. I liked testing. It is technical and also analysis. Then I moved to automation and process work.
My English is Intermediate. B1. I can speak about my work. I use short sentences.

items.q: What does senior mean for you?
items.a: I do not only write tests. I own the QA path: requirements, what to automate, framework, CI, and root cause. I care that the suite is trusted.
Web and API automation with TypeScript and Playwright. Also QA process: docs, regression, and CI.
Live coding on a whiteboard is my weak part. Real automation work is stronger. I keep solutions simple: arrays, objects, loops, map and filter, async await.
SaaS. I was the process QA. I built QA process, docs, and regression. Then UI and API automation with TypeScript and Playwright. Tests in Jenkins. Localization testing for many languages.
A B2B payment platform. I was in Access and Identity. Clients, accounts, roles and permissions. Web, API, SQL, integrations. I built a Playwright framework and put it in Jenkins.
A marketplace. I was the only QA on the team. Web and APIs. I started automation there with Java, Selenium and REST Assured. I used SQL. I also did QA notifications.
I was the first QA on a project. I built the process, docs, and regression. Then I added automation and CI/CD.
I look at requirements early. I ask about unclear cases before coding is done. This stops some bugs. On FRACTAL this was part of my job.

items.q: How do you investigate a bug?
items.a: First I reproduce the bug. Then I check logs, API, network and DB. I look for the root cause, not only the bug. I ask a developer if I need help.

items.q: How do you write a bug report?
items.a: I write steps, expected and actual. I add environment, logs, network or API body if it helps. A good bug is easy to reproduce.

items.q: How do you work with deadlines?
items.a: I look at priority and risk first. If I cannot finish all work, I say it early.

items.q: How do you communicate with the team?
items.a: I write in messenger. If it is complex, I call. I explain clearly with the info people need.

items.q: How do you work with developers?
items.a: I bring facts: steps, logs, API, DB. I do not only say it is broken. We look at the cause together.
I look at risk and what can break users. Smoke first. Then critical flows. Then extra cases if there is time.
Retest checks the fix. Regression checks that old flows still work. Automation helps regression stay short.

items.q: What test design do you use?
items.a: Equivalence partitioning and boundary values. Also decision tables, state transition, pairwise, and edge cases. I pick the method for the risk.
I test first what hurts users or money or access. Low risk can wait. This helps with deadlines.
Yes. I explore when the spec is thin or the UI is new. I still write down what I found.
Yes. At FRACTAL I did localization and manual checks for many languages.

items.q: How do you decide manual vs auto?
items.a: If the flow is stable and we run it often, I automate. If it is a one-time check or a very new UI, I test manual first.

items.q: What is a good test case?
items.a: It has a clear goal, preconditions, steps, and expected result. It is easy for another QA to run.
Now I use TypeScript and Playwright. I test UI and API. I use POM. Tests run in Jenkins. I use Allure for reports. At RIA.com I used Java, Selenium and Maven.
Playwright is my current work stack. Auto-wait is better. I can do UI and API in one tool. I still know Selenium from RIA.com.

items.q: How do you build a test framework?
items.a: TypeScript, Playwright, OOP and POM. Fixtures for setup. Tests in Jenkins. Allure for reports. At Clear Junction I built the framework from scratch.
Page Object Model. Locators and actions live in the page class. The test calls the page. If the UI changes, I fix one page, not every test.
Fixtures give a ready context to the test. Browser, page, logged user. I do not copy setup in every test.
I log in once. I save cookies and local storage. Next tests start already logged in. This makes the suite faster and more stable.

items.q: How do you handle login in tests?
items.a: I prefer login once with storageState or API login. I do not click the login form in every test if I can avoid it.
I like role, label, and test id. I avoid long CSS and nth. The locator must stay after a small UI change.
Yes. Role and name are close to how a user sees the page. If there is no good role, I use a test id.
I do not like sleep. I wait for the element or the response. Sleep hides the real problem and makes tests slow.
Stable and important flows. Regression. Critical UI and API paths. Repeated setup. The test must work in CI.
I do not automate a flow that changes every day. I do not automate a one-time check. First I ask: will CI run this next month?
API is faster and more stable for business rules. UI is for the user path. I like both. Sometimes I assert through API after a UI step.

items.q: How do you test API in Playwright?
items.a: I use APIRequest. I send the request. I check status, headers and body. I can also log in by API.
It checks the business result. User created. Status 201. Total in cart. Not only that a button was clicked.

items.q: How do you work with flaky tests?
items.a: I check locators, timing, test data and the environment. I look at the trace. I look for the real cause. I do not add a wait and hope.

items.q: How do you debug a failed test?
items.a: I open the trace, screenshot, and error. I check network and API. I run the test locally. Then I fix locator, data, or the wait.
Yes, when tests do not share data. If the account or cart is shared, I use one worker. I did this in a Playwright test task.
I can work with frames and with cookies. storageState also keeps cookies. I use this for auth.
I need data I can control. I create it by API or SQL when I can. Shared dirty data makes tests flaky.

items.q: Smoke vs full regression in automation?
items.a: Smoke is small and fast. It runs on a pull request. Full regression can run at night. I used this idea with Jenkins jobs.

items.q: What Jenkins jobs did you use?
items.a: Merge request checks. Branch jobs. Nightly. The job should fail the pipeline if critical tests fail.

items.q: Allure — what do you look at?
items.a: I look which test failed and why. I look at steps, attachments, and if it is a product bug or a test bug.
Yes. Page classes, fixtures, small helpers. The test file should read like a story, not like a big script.
Page holds locators and UI actions. Fixture holds setup. Helper is a small shared function. I keep them separate so the suite stays clear.

items.q: How do you review generated tests?
items.a: I read locators, waits, and asserts. I check if the test matches the risk. I never merge AI code without reading it.

items.q: Do you use AI in QA?
items.a: I use Cursor every day. I read all generated code. I use it to refactor tests, debug failures, search for cases, and draft test docs. I still own locators, waits and asserts.

items.q: Java Selenium vs Playwright — what changed?
items.a: At RIA.com I used Java, Selenium and Maven. Now at work I use TypeScript and Playwright. The idea is the same: stable locators, POM, CI. The tool is different.
No. It is a test task. Playwright and TypeScript. I check the business result, not a fixed click path. I keep it in my GitHub portfolio.

items.q: How do you test UI that changes a lot?
items.a: I assert the result, not one click path. In a test task I used a heuristic walker for A/B UI. At work I prefer stable locators and API checks.
I use Postman and Playwright API. I check status codes, headers and auth. I also do negative cases. Sometimes I check API data with DB.
401 means no auth. The token is missing or bad. 403 means you are logged in, but you have no permission. I test both.
I check login, token or cookie, expired session, and no token. I check that a closed API returns 401 or 403.
Bad body. Missing field. Wrong type. No auth. No permission. I check the status and the error body.
Postman is good to explore and to share a collection. Playwright API is good in CI next to UI tests. I use both. I also used Newman.
Yes, in my Java time. Together with Selenium at RIA.com. Now I use Playwright API more.
I use SQL as a QA. I check data, prepare test data and investigate bugs. Joins, filters, aggregation. I am not a DBA.
If the API says the user is created, I can check the row in DB. If they do not match, I have a real bug.

items.q: What CI tools did you use?
items.a: I use Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions. I work with Git every day: branches, PRs and review.
Yes. I use branches and PRs. If there is a conflict, I resolve it and check tests still run.

items.q: What do you put in a PR?
items.a: A short why. What I tested. If tests are in CI, the job should be green.
Yes. I worked on a B2B payment platform. I tested Access and Identity: clients, accounts, roles and permissions. I also tested APIs and integrations. I am not a payment-provider-flow specialist.
Yes. I tested how services talk: API, webhooks-style flows, and data in DB. I check status and the final state.
I used logs and tools like Grafana, Kibana, Datadog, Prometheus. I use them to find why a test or a bug happened.
I did functional testing on mobile, for example registration. I am not a mobile automation specialist. I do not claim Appium.
I do not have strong commercial experience with GraphQL, Kafka, or Docker as a main duty. I have study notes. My work CI was Jenkins.
I am not a performance specialist. I watch response times in API and monitoring. Load testing is not my main skill.
On GitHub. Repo note-Advanced-web-automation-course. 38 sections. Networking, testing, Git, Jenkins, SQL, APIs, Java and JS. There is a glossary. I also have a short Notes page on this site.
POM keeps locators and actions in one place. If the UI changes, I fix the page, not every test. I used POM in Playwright test tasks and at work.

items.q: Which HTTP codes do you use as a QA?
items.a: 200 is OK. 201 is created. 400 is bad request. 401 is no auth. 403 is no permission. 404 is not found. 500 is server error. I check the code and the body. I keep a full list in my glossary.

items.q: GET vs POST vs PUT vs PATCH vs DELETE?
items.a: GET reads. POST creates. PUT replaces. PATCH updates a part. DELETE removes. I check the method and if the data changed.
You can call it again and the result stays the same. GET is idempotent. POST often is not. I think about this in API tests.
Cookie can go to the server. localStorage stays in the browser. Session storage dies with the tab. storageState can save cookies and storage for tests.
The test life cycle: plan, cases, run, report, close. I also work in Agile: sprint, risk, and fast feedback.
Smoke is a short check that the build works. Sanity is a short check of one change. I keep smoke small so CI is fast.
Equivalence partitioning: I pick one value from a group. Boundary value: I test the edge, like min and max. I use this for forms and API fields.
Decision table is for many rules together. State transition is for status flows. I use them when if-else in the product is complex.
A stub gives a ready answer. A mock also checks how you call it. I use this idea when API or UI is not ready. I wrote this in my testing notes.

items.q: Do you know Docker and Kubernetes?
items.a: I have study notes on Docker and Kubernetes. My CI at work was Jenkins. I do not claim K8s as a commercial duty.
A test that fails and then passes with no product change. The cause is often locator, timing, data, or the environment.

items.q: What is a test pyramid for you?
items.a: More fast API and unit-like checks. Fewer slow UI E2E. E2E still needed for the user path. I do not only write UI tests.

items.q: What do you usually ask a recruiter?
items.a: I ask about the QA team size. I ask how many people do manual tests and how many do automation. I ask if there is a QA Lead. I ask how QA works with developers. I ask about automation coverage. I ask what they expect in the first one to three months. I ask about the interview steps. I ask about English. I ask how much time is manual and how much is automation.
I ask how big is QA. Who is the QA Lead. Who reviews test PRs.

items.q: What stack does the team use?
items.a: I ask if they use Playwright or Selenium. TypeScript or Java. This helps me see if I fit.
I ask what is already automated. What is still manual. What they want in three months.

items.q: How do you work with developers?
items.a: I ask if QA joins planning. If we see PRs early. Shift-left needs this.
I ask how many steps. Is there live coding. Is there a test task. I say live coding is my weaker part. I am honest.
I ask if daily English is needed. My level is B1. I can speak about work in short sentences.
I prefer remote. I can relocate. I ask about the format of the team.

footer: Mykhailo Kovalenko · Senior General QA Engineer
